Welcome back to ‘Healthy Living’. I’m Jane, and today we’re talking about something that affects millions of older adults every year – falls at home. According to the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents, one in three people over 65 will experience a fall each year. Many of these happen in the home, but most are preventable. Today, I’ll share practical tips to make your home safer.

First, let’s talk about lighting. Poor lighting is a major cause of trips and stumbles. As we age, our eyes need more light to see obstacles. So, increase the wattage of bulbs in hallways, stairs, and bathrooms. Use night lights in bedrooms and bathrooms – they cost very little to run and can prevent a midnight fall. Also, put a torch by your bedside in case of a power cut. And make sure light switches are at the top and bottom of stairs, so you never have to walk in the dark.

Second, flooring. Loose rugs and carpets are dangerous. If you have rugs, either remove them or fix them down with double‑sided tape or a non‑slip backing. Don’t use small mats that can bunch up. In the kitchen, use anti‑fatigue mats that have a textured surface. Also, avoid waxing floors – they become slippery. If you spill water or grease, wipe it up immediately.

Now, stairs. Stairs are where many serious falls happen. Install handrails on both sides of the staircase, even if you only need one side – having two gives you extra support. Check that handrails are securely fixed and run the full length of the stairs. Also, mark the edge of each step with contrasting tape – bright yellow or white against dark carpet. This helps you see where one step ends and the next begins. Never leave objects on the stairs – no shoes, no books, no shopping bags.

Bathrooms are another high‑risk area. Wet tiles are slippery. Use non‑slip mats inside and outside the shower or bath. Install grab bars near the toilet and in the shower – not towel rails, which aren’t strong enough. A shower chair and a handheld showerhead allow you to bathe sitting down. Also, consider a raised toilet seat – it makes sitting and standing easier. The ideal water temperature for a bath is 37‑38 degrees Celsius – too hot can make you dizzy.

In the living room, arrange furniture so there are clear pathways. Remove low coffee tables or electrical cords that cross walkways. Secure loose wires behind furniture or use cord covers. Keep frequently used items within easy reach – don’t store your favourite mug on a high shelf. If you need to reach something high, use a stable step stool with handrails, never a chair.

What about medication? Some medicines can cause dizziness or drowsiness. These include blood pressure pills, sleeping tablets, and some antidepressants. If you’ve recently started a new medication and feel unsteady, talk to your doctor. They might adjust the dose or change the prescription. Also, have your eyes checked every year – poor vision leads to misjudging distances.

Exercise is also protective. Strength and balance exercises reduce fall risk. Simple things like standing on one leg while brushing your teeth, or walking heel‑to‑toe in a straight line. Tai chi and yoga are excellent. Many community centres offer free or low‑cost classes for seniors. Even 15 minutes a day makes a difference.

Finally, what to do if you do fall? Don’t panic. If you’re not hurt, roll onto your side, push up into a crawling position, and crawl to a sturdy chair. Use the chair to pull yourself up. If you’re hurt or can’t get up, try to attract attention – shout, use a whistle, or if you have a personal alarm pendant, press it. Keep a phone or mobile within reach at all times. Some people also give a spare key to a neighbour.

To summarise: improve lighting, secure rugs, install grab bars, clear clutter, check medications, and stay active. These simple changes can keep you independent and safe. Next week, we’ll talk about kitchen safety – knives, hot surfaces, and food hygiene. Until then, stay safe.

But the state pension alone won’t give you a comfortable retirement. You need private pensions and savings. The most common is a workplace pension – your employer must automatically enrol you if you’re over 22 and earn more than £10,000 per year. You contribute 5% of your salary, your employer adds 3%, and the government adds tax relief. That total 8% goes into your pension pot. If you’re self‑employed, you need a personal pension – a SIPP or stakeholder pension.

Now, how much should you save? A common rule of thumb is to save half your age as a percentage of your salary, starting from when you begin saving. For example, if you start at 40, save 20% of your salary each year. If you start at 50, save 25%. That’s a lot, but remember that includes employer contributions. So a 50‑year‑old earning £40,000 would need to put away £10,000 per year – that’s £833 per month. With employer match, you might only need to contribute £500 yourself.

But many people can’t save that much. So what can you do? First, increase your workplace pension contributions gradually. Every time you get a pay rise, put half of the increase into your pension. You won’t miss it. Second, use a Lifetime ISA if you’re under 40. The government adds 25% bonus up to £4,000 per year. That’s free money. But note – you can’t access a Lifetime ISA until age 60 without penalty.

Third, pay off expensive debt first. If you have credit card debt at 20% interest, paying that off is better than saving for retirement because the interest you save is higher than investment returns. Once debt is cleared, redirect those payments to your pension.

Investment choices matter too. If you’re in your 40s, you can afford more risk – a mix of 70% shares and 30% bonds. In your 50s, shift to 50‑50. In your 60s, more bonds and cash. Most workplace pensions offer default funds called ‘lifestyle funds’ that automatically adjust as you age. But check the fees – even 1% in fees can reduce your final pot by 20% over 20 years. Aim for funds with fees below 0.5%.

What about property? Many people think their house is their pension. That’s risky. Yes, you could downsize and release equity, but moving costs are high – estate agent fees, legal fees, stamp duty. And you still need somewhere to live. Equity release schemes allow you to take money from your home without moving, but interest rolls up, and your heirs get less. It’s a last resort.

Another option is working longer. Delaying retirement by just three years – from 65 to 68 – can increase your pension income by 30% because you contribute more and draw it for fewer years. Even working part‑time in retirement makes a big difference. Many people find they enjoy working a few days a week.

Let me give you an example. Sarah is 50, earns £45,000, and has £50,000 in her pension. If she continues contributing 8%  and retires at 67, with 4% investment growth after inflation, she’ll have about £180,000. That gives an annual income of about £7,200 plus state pension of £11,500 – total £18,700. That’s below the £25,000 she wants. But if she increases contributions to 15% of salary, her pot grows to £280,000, giving £11,200 per year from her pension – total £22,700. Still short. If she also delays retirement to 68, she reaches £25,000. So it’s possible with effort.

Finally, take action today. Log into your pension, check the balance and fees. Increase your contribution by 1% tomorrow – you won’t notice it in your pay packet. And speak to a financial advisor if your situation is complex. Thank you. I’ll now take questions.

Hello, and welcome to ‘Gardening with Alan’. Today we’re talking about growing your own vegetables – even if you only have a tiny balcony or a small paved yard. You don’t need a huge allotment. With some clever techniques, you can grow fresh tomatoes, lettuce, herbs, and even potatoes in containers. Let’s get started.

First, assess your space and sunlight. Most vegetables need at least six hours of direct sunlight per day. So observe your balcony or patio – where does the sun fall? South‑facing spots are best, east‑facing gets morning sun, west‑facing gets afternoon sun. North‑facing is too shady for most vegetables, but you can grow leafy greens like spinach or chard there. If you have a very small space, use vertical space – hanging baskets, wall‑mounted planters, or a ladder shelf.

Now, choose the right containers. Don’t use tiny pots – they dry out too quickly. For tomatoes or peppers, you need a container at least 30 cm wide and 30 cm deep. For root vegetables like carrots, depth matters – at least 25 cm. You can use plastic buckets, wooden crates, or fabric grow bags. Make sure there are drainage holes at the bottom. Put a saucer underneath to catch excess water, especially if you’re on a balcony where drips might annoy neighbours.

What about compost? Don’t use garden soil – it’s too heavy and may contain pests. Buy multipurpose or container compost from a garden centre. For best results, mix in some slow‑release fertiliser pellets – they feed the plants for three months. Also, add a handful of vermiculite or perlite to improve drainage and aeration. Water the compost before planting so it’s evenly moist.

Now, what to grow? For beginners, I recommend salad leaves. Cut‑and‑come‑again lettuce, rocket, and spinach are very easy. You sow seeds directly into a shallow container – about 2 cm apart. After three to four weeks, you can start harvesting the outer leaves, and the plant will keep producing for months. A 30 cm pot can feed a family of four salad for weeks.

Next, tomatoes. Cherry tomatoes are better for containers than large beefsteak types. Buy young plants from a garden centre in May – growing from seed is harder. Plant one tomato plant per 30 cm pot. You’ll need a cane or small trellis for support. Water daily in hot weather, and feed with liquid tomato fertiliser once a week once the flowers appear. You’ll get fruit from July to September.

Herbs are also excellent for small spaces. Basil, parsley, chives, mint, and thyme all grow well in pots. Mint is very vigorous – grow it alone in its own pot, or it will take over everything. Basil loves warmth – put it in the sunniest spot. Harvest regularly to encourage bushy growth. Fresh herbs from your balcony taste much better than dried ones from a supermarket.

What about root vegetables? Radishes are the fastest – you can harvest in four weeks. Sow seeds directly into a deep pot, thin them to 3 cm apart. Carrots need deeper pots – at least 25 cm deep. Choose short varieties like ‘Parmex’ or ‘Paris Market’ – they grow into round balls rather than long roots. Sow seeds thinly, and keep soil consistently moist.

Potatoes? Yes, you can grow potatoes in a large bucket or a special potato grow bag. Place a layer of compost at the bottom, put two or three seed potatoes on top, cover with 10 cm of compost. As the stems grow, add more compost – this is called ‘earthing up’. After about 12 weeks, when the leaves turn yellow, tip out the bucket and harvest new potatoes. Delicious.

Now, watering is critical. Containers dry out faster than ground soil. In summer, you might need to water every day, or even twice a day for small pots. Stick your finger into the compost – if it’s dry up to your second knuckle, water. Water thoroughly until water runs out of the drainage holes. Avoid watering the leaves – that encourages fungal diseases. Water the soil directly.

Feeding is also important. After about six weeks, the initial fertiliser will be used up. Then apply a liquid fertiliser every two weeks. Tomato fertiliser is high in potassium, good for flowering plants. For leafy greens, use a balanced fertiliser or one higher in nitrogen. Never feed a dry plant – water first, then feed, to avoid burning roots.

Pests? Aphids  are common. You can spray them with a mixture of water and a few drops of washing‑up liquid. Or buy a small pack of ladybirds – they eat aphids. Slugs can climb containers, so put a ring of copper tape around the pot – slugs get a mild electric shock and turn away.

Finally, don’t be discouraged if a plant fails. Gardening is about learning. Start with just two or three pots – maybe lettuce, a tomato, and basil. Once you succeed, add more. And remember, something you grew yourself always tastes better. Happy gardening.

Good evening, everyone. I’m Claire, a paramedic with 12 years of experience. Tonight, I’ll teach you basic first aid for the most common emergencies that happen at home – choking, burns, bleeding, and cardiac arrest. These skills can save a life while you wait for an ambulance. Let’s start with choking.

Choking happens when a piece of food or a small object blocks the airway. The person cannot speak, breathe, or cough effectively. They might clutch their throat – that’s the universal sign. First, ask ‘Are you choking?’ If they can cough or speak, encourage them to keep coughing – do not interfere. But if they cannot cough or speak, you need to act.

For adults and children over one year, stand behind them, put one arm across their chest for support, and lean them forward. Give up to five back blows between the shoulder blades – use the heel of your hand. After each blow, check if the blockage is dislodged. If not, do abdominal thrusts – the Heimlich manoeuvre. Make a fist with one hand, place it just above the navel, grasp it with your other hand, and pull sharply inwards and upwards. Do up to five thrusts. Alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unconscious. If they become unconscious, start CPR.

For babies under one year, do not do abdominal thrusts – you could damage their organs. Instead, hold the baby face down along your forearm, with their head lower than their chest. Give up to five back blows with the heel of your hand. Then turn the baby over and give five chest thrusts – two fingers in the centre of the chest, pushing down about 4 cm. Repeat until the object comes out.

Now, burns. First, cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Do not use ice – ice can cause further damage. Do not apply butter, toothpaste, or oil – these trap heat and increase infection risk. After cooling, cover the burn with cling film or a clean plastic bag – this protects it and reduces pain. For electrical or chemical burns, do not cool with water if the chemical reacts violently – instead, brush off dry chemicals and then irrigate with water. Seek medical help for any burn larger than the person’s palm, or on the face, hands, feet, or genitals.

Next, severe bleeding. Your priority is to stop the bleeding. Put on disposable gloves if available – but if not, use a plastic bag over your hands. Apply direct pressure to the wound using a clean cloth or dressing. Do not remove any object that is embedded – like a knife or glass shard – because that could worsen bleeding. Instead, apply pressure around the object. If blood soaks through, do not remove the first cloth – add another on top. Raise the injured limb above the heart if no fracture is suspected. If bleeding is life‑threatening, use a tourniquet only if you have training – otherwise, just keep pressing.

Now, the most important: cardiac arrest.

transcript.speaker: signs
transcript.text:
the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. First, check for danger – are you safe? Then, check response – tap their shoulders and shout ‘Are you okay?’ If no response, shout for help. Ask someone to call 999  and to bring an automated external defibrillator  if available. Then open the airway – tilt the head back and lift the chin. Look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If they are not breathing or only gasping, start CPR.

Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest . Place your other hand on top, interlock your fingers. Keep your arms straight and your shoulders over your hands. Push down at least 5 cm – about 2 inches – at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. That’s the beat of the song ‘Stayin’ Alive’ by the Bee Gees. Let the chest rise fully between compressions. Do 30 compressions, then 2 rescue breaths. If you’re not trained in rescue breaths or are unwilling, do hands‑only CPR – just compressions.

For rescue breaths: tilt the head, lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs, and blow for one second – you should see the chest rise. Do two breaths, then back to compressions. Continue until an AED arrives, the person shows signs of life, or you are too exhausted to continue.

If an AED arrives, turn it on and follow the voice prompts. Place the pads on the bare chest as shown – one on the right upper chest, one on the left lower side. The machine will analyse the heart rhythm. If it says ‘shock advised’, make sure no one is touching the person, then press the shock button. Then immediately resume CPR. The AED will guide you.

Finally, when an ambulance arrives, tell the paramedics what happened – when did the person collapse, did you see what caused it, how many shocks did the AED give? Also, hand over any medications the person was taking.

Remember, first aid is not about perfection – it’s about doing something. A rough CPR is better than no CPR. The survival rate for out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest is less than 10% without bystander CPR, but it can triple with immediate action. So please, practice these skills. Your local Red Cross runs courses. I’ll now take questions.

First, understand your biggest energy users. In a typical UK home, heating accounts for about 55% of your bill, followed by hot water , appliances , lighting , and cooking . So focus on heating first. Turn down your thermostat by just one degree – from 20°C to 19°C – and you’ll save about 10% on your heating bill. Most people don’t notice the difference. Also, set your heating to come on only when you’re home. A smart thermostat can learn your schedule, but even a basic timer works.

Second, draughtproofing. Heat escapes through gaps around windows, doors, floorboards, and chimneys. Draught excluders – those long fabric tubes – cost about £5 each and can stop cold air coming under doors. Self‑adhesive foam strips for windows cost about £3 per window. Seal your letterbox with a brush strip. And if you have a chimney, use a chimney balloon  when not in use. These small investments pay back within one winter.

Third, radiator efficiency. Many radiators have air trapped inside – that stops them heating fully. Bleed your radiators once a year. You’ll need a radiator key . Turn off the heating, wait for radiators to cool, then open the valve at the top – you’ll hear a hiss. When water comes out, close it. That can improve heat output by 20%. Also, don’t put furniture in front of radiators – that absorbs heat. And put reflective foil behind radiators on external walls to bounce heat back into the room. Foil costs about £5 per roll.

Fourth, water heating. Your hot water cylinder should be well insulated. A cylinder jacket costs about £15 and pays for itself in six months. Set your hot water thermostat to 60°C – that’s hot enough for hygiene but not wasteful. And take showers instead of baths – a five‑minute shower uses about a third of the water of a bath. Install a water‑efficient showerhead – some use 8 litres per minute instead of 15.

Now, appliances. Many devices draw power even when turned off – this is called ‘vampire power’ or standby power. Your TV, computer, phone charger, microwave, and games console all consume electricity when plugged in but not in use. Turn them off at the socket. Use a power strip with a switch – one click turns off five devices. This can save £30‑£50 per year.

Washing machines and dishwashers: always run a full load, and use the eco mode. Eco cycles use lower temperature and longer soak times, which cleans just as well for most loads. Wash clothes at 30°C instead of 40°C – that uses 40% less electricity. And air‑dry clothes instead of using a tumble dryer. A tumble dryer is one of the most expensive appliances to run – about 70p per load. A drying rack or outdoor line costs nothing.

Refrigerators and freezers: don’t set them colder than needed – fridge at 4°C, freezer at -18°C. Keep the coils at the back clean – dust makes them work harder. And ensure the door seals are tight – put a £5 note in the door and close it; if you can pull it out easily, the seal needs replacing. Also, let hot food cool before putting it in the fridge – that reduces the fridge’s work.

transcript.speaker: lighting
transcript.text:
replace all old incandescent or halogen bulbs with LEDs. LEDs use 85% less electricity and last 15 times longer. A single LED bulb costs about £2 and saves about £10 per year on electricity. If you have 10 bulbs, that’s £100 per year. Also, turn off lights when you leave a room – it’s a simple habit.

Finally, cooking. Use a slow cooker, microwave, or air fryer instead of the oven when possible. An oven uses 2‑3 kWh per hour; a microwave uses 0.6 kWh for the same meal. Boil only the water you need in a kettle – if you fill it to the max for one cup, you waste energy. Use a lid on pots – it traps heat and speeds cooking.

Many energy suppliers offer free or discounted home energy audits. They come to your house and identify where you’re losing heat. Some also offer grants for insulation or boiler upgrades, especially for low‑income households or those over 70. Check your supplier’s website.

To summarise, you don’t need to spend thousands. Start with the thermostat – turn it down one degree. Bleed your radiators. Switch to LEDs. And turn appliances off at the socket. If you do all these, you could cut your bill by 20‑30%. That’s real money. Next week, we’ll talk about saving water. Until then, stay warm and save wisely.

Good evening. I’m Dr. Sarah Jones, a clinical psychologist. Tonight we’re talking about stress – something everyone in this room has experienced. Stress isn’t always bad. The right amount of stress – ‘eustress’ – helps us perform better. It’s the stress before a presentation or a sports match that sharpens our focus. But chronic, unrelenting stress damages our health. So let’s understand how stress works and what we can do about it.

First, the biology. When you perceive a threat, your brain’s amygdala sends a distress signal to the hypothalamus, which activates the sympathetic nervous system – your ‘fight or flight’ response. Your adrenal glands release adrenaline and cortisol. Your heart rate increases, blood pressure rises, and glucose is released for energy. In a real emergency – like a car speeding toward you – this saves your life. The problem is that modern stressors – work deadlines, traffic jams, money worries – trigger the same response, but we can’t fight or flee. So the cortisol stays elevated.

Chronic high cortisol leads to problems: disrupted sleep, weight gain , weakened immune system, high blood pressure, and anxiety. It can also shrink the hippocampus – the brain’s memory centre. So managing stress isn’t just about feeling better – it’s about long‑term health.

So what can we do? Let’s start with immediate, in‑the‑moment techniques. Deep breathing is the most effective. When you’re stressed, you tend to take shallow, rapid breaths. That signals your brain that something is wrong. Instead, try box breathing: inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. Repeat for two minutes. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system – the ‘rest and digest’ system. It lowers heart rate within minutes.

Another quick technique is grounding. Look around and name five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This pulls your attention away from anxious thoughts and into the present moment. It works especially well for panic attacks.

Now, longer‑term strategies. Exercise is one of the most powerful stress reducers. Aerobic exercise – walking, jogging, swimming – releases endorphins, natural painkillers that also improve mood. Just 20 minutes of moderate exercise reduces cortisol for several hours. And regular exercise improves sleep, which in turn reduces stress. Aim for 150 minutes per week – that’s 30 minutes, five days a week. Even a brisk walk counts.

Sleep is critical. Stress makes it hard to sleep, and poor sleep increases stress – a vicious cycle. Set a consistent bedtime and wake time, even on weekends. Avoid screens for an hour before bed – blue light suppresses melatonin. Instead, read a paper book, listen to calm music, or take a warm bath. Keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet. If you can’t sleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something boring until you feel tired – don’t just lie there worrying.

Social support is a buffer against stress. People with strong social networks have lower cortisol responses to stressors. Even one close friend you can call makes a difference. But be careful – complaining together without problem‑solving can increase stress . So talk about solutions, not just problems.

Cognitive techniques are also powerful. Stress often comes from our thoughts, not events. For example, you might think ‘I have to be perfect’ or ‘everything is going wrong’. Challenge those thoughts.

transcript.speaker: ask
transcript.text:
‘Is that really true? What’s the evidence? What would I tell a friend in this situation?’ This is the basis of cognitive behavioural therapy. You can learn these skills from books or free online courses.

Time management reduces stress. Many of us feel overwhelmed because we have too many tasks. Use the ‘Eisenhower Matrix’: sort tasks into four boxes – urgent and important , important but not urgent , urgent but not important , and neither . Most stress comes from urgent but not important tasks – like responding to every email immediately. Learn to say no.

Mindfulness meditation has strong evidence. It doesn’t mean emptying your mind – it means paying attention to the present moment without judgement. Apps like Headspace or Calm offer free beginner courses. Just 10 minutes a day for eight weeks can reduce anxiety and improve emotional regulation. Even mindful eating – paying full attention to each bite – can be a form of practice.

Finally, don’t ignore professional help. If stress is interfering with your work, relationships, or sleep for more than a few weeks, see your GP. They can recommend talking therapy – often available free on the NHS . In some cases, medication like SSRIs may help, especially if stress has become depression or anxiety disorder.

Let me summarise: stress is normal, but chronic stress is harmful. Use deep breathing for immediate relief. Exercise regularly, prioritise sleep, and nurture social connections. Challenge unhelpful thoughts. And seek help if you need it. You don’t have to manage alone.

Now, I’ll take questions. Does anyone have a personal stress challenge they’d like to discuss?

Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to our ‘Grow Your Own Fruit’ talk. Many people think fruit is too difficult to grow at home, but with the right varieties and basic care, you can harvest strawberries, raspberries, apples, and even pears from a small garden or patio. Let’s start with the easiest fruit – strawberries.

Strawberries are perfect for beginners. You can buy bare‑root plants in winter or potted plants in spring. Plant them in a sunny spot with well‑drained soil. Space plants 30 cm apart. They produce fruit from June to August. The key is to water consistently – irregular watering leads to small, misshapen berries. Put straw or a special strawberry mat under the developing fruit to keep them off the soil and prevent rot. After fruiting, cut off the old leaves and runners . Those runners can be rooted to make new plants for free. A single plant can produce 300‑500 grams of fruit.

Now, raspberries. There are two types: summer‑fruiting  and autumn‑fruiting . Summer varieties fruit on canes grown the previous year – you need to support them on wires or a trellis. After harvest, cut down the old canes to ground level. Autumn varieties fruit on the current year’s canes – you can cut all canes to the ground in winter, and new ones will fruit the next summer/autumn. Raspberries need rich, moist soil and a sunny spot. Protect from birds with netting – otherwise, you’ll lose half your crop. A row of 5 metres can yield 5‑10 kg per year.

Blueberries are a bit more demanding. They need acidic soil . If your soil is alkaline, grow them in pots with ericaceous compost. They also need constant moisture – never let them dry out. And they need at least two different varieties for cross‑pollination, otherwise fruit set is poor. Popular varieties include ‘Bluecrop’ and ‘Patriot’. Blueberries are high in antioxidants and very expensive in shops, so growing your own saves money.

Now, tree fruit – apples and pears. For a small garden, choose dwarf or semi‑dwarf rootstocks. M27 is very dwarf , perfect for pots. M26 is semi‑dwarf . Avoid standard rootstocks like M25 – they grow 6‑8 metres tall. Most apples need a pollination partner – a different variety that flowers at the same time. Crab apples are excellent pollinators. If you only have space for one tree, buy a ‘family tree’ – three varieties grafted onto one trunk.

Plant fruit trees in winter when they are dormant. Dig a hole twice the width of the root ball, but no deeper. You want the graft union  above soil level. Add a stake to support the tree for the first two years. Water well for the first year, but after that, only during droughts. Prune in winter to maintain an open, goblet shape – this lets light and air into the centre. Remove dead, diseased, or crossing branches.

Pests and diseases – birds are the biggest nuisance. Net your fruit as it ripens. For codling moth , hang pheromone traps in spring to reduce mating. For aphids, encourage ladybirds by planting marigolds and dill nearby. For powdery mildew , improve air circulation and avoid high‑nitrogen fertiliser.

Finally, harvesting. Strawberries and raspberries are best picked on a dry day, in the morning after dew has dried, when they are fully coloured. Eat or freeze within 24 hours. Apples are ready when the pips have turned brown and the fruit comes off with a gentle twist. Pears are trickier – they ripen off the tree. Pick them when they are still firm but the colour has changed, then store in a cool place to ripen.

Now, what about containers? If you have a balcony, grow strawberries in hanging baskets, blueberries in a 30‑cm pot, and a dwarf apple in a 50‑cm pot. Use a loam‑based compost like John Innes No. 3, and feed with a slow‑release fertiliser. Water daily in summer – containers dry out fast.

Remember, fruit growing is a long‑term investment. You may not get a big harvest in the first year, but by year three, you’ll have more than you can eat. And nothing tastes better than a sun‑warmed strawberry from your own garden. I’ll now take questions.

Good evening. I’m Anna, a financial advisor. Tonight I’ll talk about budgeting – something many people find boring or intimidating, but it’s the foundation of financial health. Without a budget, you don’t know where your money goes. With a budget, you can save for holidays, emergencies, or retirement. Let’s start with a simple method – the 50/30/20 rule.

The 50/30/20 rule is easy: 50% of your after‑tax income goes to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings and debt repayment. Needs include rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, transport, minimum loan payments, and insurance. Wants include dining out, hobbies, subscriptions, travel, and entertainment. Savings include emergency fund, retirement, and extra debt payments beyond the minimum.

For example, if you take home £2,000 per month, you should spend no more than £1,000 on needs, up to £600 on wants, and save at least £400. Adjust the percentages if you live in an expensive city – some people need 60% for needs, so they save 10% and wants 30%. The key is to track and adjust.

So how do you track? Start with a month of logging every expense. Use a notebook, a spreadsheet, or an app like YNAB or Emma. At the end of the month, categorise your spending. You’ll likely be surprised – many people underestimate how much they spend on coffee, takeaways, or subscriptions. That £3 coffee every workday is £60 per month – £720 per year.

After tracking, create a budget. Write down your fixed expenses – rent, council tax, utilities, phone bill, insurance, debt minimums. These are non‑negotiable. Then variable expenses – groceries, petrol, clothing, entertainment. Set a realistic limit for each. For groceries, a single adult might spend £150‑£250 per month; a family of four £400‑£600.

Now, savings. The first priority is an emergency fund – 3 to 6 months of living expenses in an easy‑access savings account. If you lose your job or have a medical emergency, this fund keeps you afloat. Start small – save £500, then £1,000. Once you have a month’s expenses, aim for three months. Keep it separate from your main account – out of sight, out of mind.

Next, pay down high‑interest debt. Credit card debt at 20% interest is an emergency – paying it off is like earning 20% guaranteed return. Use the ‘avalanche method’: list debts by interest rate . Pay minimum on all, then put every extra pound toward the highest‑rate debt. Or use the ‘snowball method’: pay smallest balance first for psychological wins. Choose whichever keeps you motivated.

After debt and emergency fund, save for specific goals – a house deposit, a car, a holiday. Use sinking funds: set aside a fixed amount each month. For a £3,000 holiday in 12 months, save £250 per month. Automate the transfer on payday – you won’t miss it.

Now, cutting costs. Many people can reduce needs: switch to a cheaper energy tariff, shop for cheaper car insurance, negotiate your broadband bill. For groceries, buy own‑brand products, plan meals, and avoid food waste. The average UK household throws away £60 of food per month. That’s £720 per year.

For wants, try a ‘no‑spend month’ – challenge yourself to spend only on needs for 30 days. No takeaways, no new clothes, no cinema. You’ll realise what you truly miss. Then reintroduce wants mindfully.

Another technique is the ‘24‑hour rule’ for impulse purchases. When you want to buy something non‑essential, wait 24 hours. Most urges fade. For expensive items, wait 30 days. If you still want it, save up – don’t use credit.

What about irregular expenses? Car repairs, Christmas gifts, annual insurance – these blow budgets if you don’t plan. Set up a ‘sinking fund’ for each: estimate the annual cost, divide by 12, and save monthly. For example, car maintenance £600 per year = £50 per month. Christmas £300 = £25 per month.

Now, technology. Use open banking apps that categorise spending automatically. Many are free. Set spending alerts – when you reach 80% of a category budget, get a notification. Some apps also round up purchases to the nearest pound and save the difference – a painless way to save.

Finally, review your budget monthly. Your income or expenses may change. Be flexible – a budget is a tool, not a prison. If you overspend one category, reduce another next month. The goal is progress, not perfection.

Let me give you a success story. Sarah, a client, earned £2,200 per month. She thought she had no money to save. After tracking, she found she spent £200 on takeaways, £150 on clothes, and £40 on unused subscriptions. She cut takeaways to £50, stopped impulse clothes buys, cancelled unused subscriptions, and saved £300 per month. In one year, she built a £3,600 emergency fund. Then she started saving for a house deposit.

Remember, small changes compound. Cutting £5 per day on lunch  saves £100 per month, £1,200 per year. Invested at 5% over 20 years, that’s over £40,000. So start today – write down your income and expenses, set a 50/30/20 budget, and automate your savings. You can do this.

Hello, and welcome to ‘Pet Talk’. I’m Rachel. Today we’re focusing on rabbits – the third most popular pet in the UK after dogs and cats, but often misunderstood. Many people think rabbits are low‑maintenance ‘starter pets’ for children. In reality, rabbits require specialised care, a large living space, and can live 8‑12 years. So let’s get into it.

First, housing. Do not keep a rabbit in a small hutch. The minimum recommended size for two rabbits is a hutch of at least 6 feet by 2 feet, attached to a run of 8 feet by 4 feet – that’s 32 square feet of exercise space. The hutch should have a solid floor  to prevent sore hocks.

transcript.speaker: bedding
transcript.text:
dust‑free hay or straw. Avoid pine or cedar shavings – they release harmful phenols. Clean the hutch weekly, and spot‑clean daily.

Rabbits are social animals – they should live in pairs or groups. A single rabbit can become depressed. The best pairing is a neutered male and a neutered female. Same‑sex pairs can work but may fight. Always neuter – it prevents cancer  and reduces aggression.

Now, diet – this is critical. A rabbit’s digestive system is delicate. The foundation is hay – unlimited, good‑quality grass hay like timothy or meadow hay. Hay provides fibre that keeps the gut moving and grinds down their continuously growing teeth. A rabbit should eat a pile of hay the size of its own body every day. Second, fresh leafy greens – about one cup per 2 kg of body weight per day. Good options: romaine lettuce, kale, coriander, parsley. Avoid iceberg lettuce  and spinach .

Third, pellets – only a small amount, about 1/8 cup per kg of body weight per day. Choose plain, high‑fibre pellets . Avoid muesli‑style mixes – rabbits pick out the sugary bits and leave the healthy parts, causing obesity and dental problems. Fourth, treats – very limited. Small pieces of carrot, apple, or banana once a week. No commercial ‘yogurt drops’ or seeds – they cause digestive blockages.

Water – fresh, clean water daily, in a heavy bowl . Change water twice a day.

Now, health. Rabbits are prey animals, so they hide illness until they are very sick. Signs of illness: not eating, small or misshapen droppings, lethargy, teeth grinding , runny nose or eyes. If a rabbit stops eating for 12 hours, it’s an emergency – they can develop ‘gut stasis’, which is often fatal. Take them to a vet immediately.

Dental problems are common because teeth grow continuously . If they don’t wear down properly, spurs develop that cut the tongue and cheeks.

transcript.speaker: symptoms
transcript.text: drooling, weight loss, not eating hay. Treatment requires anaesthesia and burring the teeth.

transcript.speaker: prevention
transcript.text: unlimited hay, chew toys .

transcript.speaker: vaccinations
transcript.text: in the UK, rabbits need annual vaccines against myxomatosis and RHD . Both are fatal and spread by insects or contact with wild rabbits. Cost is about £50 per year. Also, ask your vet about parasite prevention – flystrike  is a summer danger. Check your rabbit’s bottom twice daily in warm weather.

transcript.speaker: handling
transcript.text: never pick up a rabbit by the ears or scruff. Support both the front and back – one hand under the chest, the other under the rump. Rabbits have fragile spines; if they kick while unsupported, they can break their own back. Children should be supervised – rabbits often dislike being held and may scratch or bite.

transcript.speaker: exercise
transcript.text:
rabbits need at least 3‑4 hours of supervised free‑range time outside their hutch daily. Indoors, bunny‑proof your home – cover electrical cords with plastic tubing, block access to toxic plants , and remove poisonous foods . Many rabbits can be litter‑trained – place a cat litter box  in a corner of their run.

What about outdoor vs indoor? Indoor rabbits live longer because they are protected from predators, temperature extremes, and parasites. If outdoors, the hutch must be predator‑proof , sheltered from wind and rain, and in shade during summer. In winter, provide extra bedding and a thermal cover. But ideally, keep rabbits indoors.

Finally, adoption – don’t buy from pet shops. Rescue centres have many rabbits needing homes. The Rabbit Welfare Association has a list of rescues. Adopting a pair already bonded saves you the hassle of bonding them yourself. Also, adults are calmer than babies and already neutered. Cost of adoption is about £50‑£100 per rabbit, including first vaccination and neutering.

To summarise: rabbits need a large living space, a companion, unlimited hay, daily greens, regular vet care, and lots of attention. They are not easy pets – but they are rewarding. If you’re not ready for a 10‑year commitment, consider volunteering at a rescue instead.

Good evening. I’m Linda from ‘Waste Not’. Tonight we’re talking about food waste – a problem that costs the average UK household about £700 per year. That’s £60 per month thrown directly into the bin. But it’s not just about money – food waste in landfill produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. So reducing waste helps your wallet and the planet. Let’s start with the scale: the UK throws away 9.5 million tonnes of food annually. 70% of that is from households, not supermarkets or restaurants. And 60% of household food waste is avoidable – food that was perfectly edible.

So why do we waste? The top reasons: we buy too much, we don’t plan meals, we misunderstand date labels, and we store food incorrectly. Let’s tackle each.

First, planning. Before shopping, check your fridge, freezer, and cupboards. Make a list of what you already have. Then plan meals for the week – breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks. Write a shopping list and stick to it. Don’t shop when hungry – impulse buys increase waste. Also, consider online shopping – you see your total cost and can review items before purchase, which reduces impulse.

Second, portion sizes. Cook only what you need. Use a portion calculator – for rice, 50‑75g dry per person; for pasta, 75‑100g; for meat, 100‑150g. If you cook extra, plan to use leftovers for lunch the next day. Leftover roast vegetables become soup. Leftover rice becomes fried rice. Stale bread becomes breadcrumbs or croutons. There are hundreds of ‘leftover recipes’ online.

Third, date labels. ‘Use by’ is about safety. Do not eat food after its use‑by date, even if it looks and smells fine – harmful bacteria can be present. This applies to meat, fish, dairy, and ready meals. ‘Best before’ is about quality. After this date, food may not taste as good but is safe to eat. This applies to dry goods like pasta, rice, cereals, tinned foods, and condiments. Many people throw away perfectly good food because they confuse the labels.

What about eggs? They can be eaten up to two days after the best‑before date if cooked thoroughly. To test: put an egg in a bowl of water – if it sinks, it’s fresh; if it floats, discard. Also, look at the egg white – if it’s runny, it’s older but still safe.

Fourth, storage. Many foods last longer if stored correctly. Potatoes, onions, and garlic should be stored in a cool, dark, dry place – not in the fridge . Keep them separate because onions release gases that make potatoes sprout faster. Apples release ethylene gas – store them away from other fruit and veg unless you want to ripen them quickly.

transcript.speaker: bananas
transcript.text:
store at room temperature; if you want to slow ripening, separate them and wrap the stem with cling film.

Leafy greens: wash and dry thoroughly, then store in a container with a paper towel to absorb moisture. They’ll last 5‑7 days instead of 2.

transcript.speaker: herbs
transcript.text: treat like flowers – trim stems, put in a glass of water, cover loosely with a plastic bag, refrigerate .

transcript.speaker: carrots
transcript.text:
remove green tops , store in a sealed bag in the fridge. They can last weeks.

Freezing is your friend. Most foods can be frozen, including milk, cheese, bread, and even eggs . Freeze fruit that’s about to go overripe – use later in smoothies or baking. Freeze vegetables after blanching  to preserve colour and nutrients. Label everything with the date. Frozen food remains safe indefinitely but quality degrades; try to use within 3‑6 months.

Now, the ‘first in, first out’ rule. When you unpack groceries, move older items to the front of the fridge or cupboard. New items go to the back. This way you use older food first. Also, keep a ‘use me first’ shelf – put items nearing their date there so you see them.

Composting is the last resort – better than landfill, but preventing waste is even better. If you have a garden, compost fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, eggshells, and tea bags. Don’t compost meat, dairy, or cooked food . If you don’t have a garden, check if your council collects food waste for anaerobic digestion – many do.

Let me give you a challenge. For one week, collect all the food you throw away. At the end of the week, analyse it. Was it leftovers? Spoiled produce? Things past their date? Then choose one change to make: plan meals, improve storage, or freeze more. You’ll likely save £10‑£20 in that week alone.

Finally, apps and tools. ‘Too Good To Go’ lets you buy surprise bags from restaurants and shops at the end of the day – cheap and reduces waste. ‘Olio’ connects neighbours to share surplus food. And the ‘Love Food Hate Waste’ website has portion calculators and storage guides.

To summarise: plan, store correctly, understand dates, use leftovers, freeze, and compost what’s left. You’ll save money, help the planet, and feel good. I’ll now take questions.

Hello, and welcome to ‘Home Fix with Dave’. Today we’re tackling common plumbing problems that you can fix yourself – without calling an expensive plumber. But first, a warning: if you’re not confident, or if the problem involves gas or major pipes, call a professional. With that said, let’s start with the most common problem – a dripping tap.

A tap that drips once per second wastes about 5,000 litres of water per year – that’s £20‑£30 on your water bill. Most dripping taps are caused by a worn washer. To fix it, first turn off the water supply – there’s usually a isolation valve under the sink. Turn it clockwise. Open the tap to drain remaining water. Then unscrew the tap handle – you may need a screwdriver or an Allen key. Under the handle, you’ll see the valve mechanism. Remove it using a spanner. Inside, you’ll find a rubber washer. If it’s cracked or flattened, replace it – a pack of washers costs about £2. Reassemble. Turn the water back on and test. If it still drips, the valve seat might be worn – that’s a bigger job.

Second problem: a running toilet. You hear water trickling long after flushing. Usually, the flapper valve  is not sealing properly. Turn off the water supply to the toilet – valve near the floor. Flush to empty the tank. Remove the flapper . Take it to a hardware store to buy a matching one – about £5. Install the new flapper, turn water on, and test. Also, check the float – if the water level is too high, water spills into the overflow tube. Adjust the float by bending the arm or turning a screw.

Third, a slow‑draining sink. Often caused by hair and soap scum in the trap – the U‑shaped pipe under the sink. Place a bucket under the trap. Unscrew the two nuts . Remove the trap and clean it out – use a wire or old toothbrush. Also, use a drain snake or a straightened coat hanger to clear the pipe going into the wall. Reassemble – don’t overtighten. Run hot water to test. For prevention, use a drain strainer to catch hair, and once a month pour a cup of baking soda followed by a cup of vinegar, wait 15 minutes, then flush with boiling water.

Fourth, low water pressure from a showerhead. Usually, the head is clogged with limescale. Unscrew the showerhead – turn counter‑clockwise. Soak it in a bowl of white vinegar for an hour. Use an old toothbrush to scrub the holes. Rinse and reattach. If pressure is still low, check the hose for kinks or the isolator valve – it might be partially closed. If you have a combi boiler, the pressure might be low – check the gauge . If below 0.5 bar, repressurise – follow boiler instructions.

Fifth, a frozen pipe in winter. This is an emergency – the pipe may burst. If you turn on a tap and only a trickle comes out, suspect a frozen pipe. Locate the frozen section – feel for a very cold spot. Open the tap nearest to the frozen area. Apply gentle heat – a hairdryer on low, a heat lamp, or towels soaked in hot water. Never use a blowtorch or open flame. Once water flows, let it run for a few minutes. To prevent future freezing, insulate pipes in unheated areas  with foam pipe insulation – cheap and easy.

Sixth, a leaking pipe joint. First, turn off the water. Dry the joint. For a compression joint, try tightening the nut – but don’t overtighten. If still leaking, you may need to replace the olive . For a soldered copper joint, you’ll need a plumber – but a temporary fix is self‑fusing silicone tape . It can hold for months. Another temporary fix: epoxy putty – knead it, press onto the leak, let cure for an hour.

Seventh, a noisy pipe – banging or knocking when you turn off a tap. That’s ‘water hammer’. It’s caused by fast‑closing valves. Fix by installing a water hammer arrestor – a small device that absorbs the shock. It screws onto the pipe near the offending tap – about £20. Or, as a temporary fix, reduce the water pressure slightly at the main valve.

Tools every homeowner should have: adjustable spanner , pipe wrench , basin wrench , plunger , plumber’s tape , and a set of screwdrivers. Total cost under £50 – far less than one plumber visit.

When to call a plumber: if you have a gas leak , if the main water pipe bursts, if you need to move pipes , or if you’ve tried everything and the problem persists. Also, if you live in a flat, check your lease – you might not be allowed to do plumbing work that affects neighbours.

To summarise: most drips, runs, and clogs are DIY. Watch YouTube videos for your specific tap or toilet model. And always turn off the water before starting. Good luck.

Next week: fixing a broken fence. Until then, happy fixing.

Good evening. I’m Dr. Emily White. Tonight I want to talk about stress – not the clinical kind, but the everyday pressure that most of us feel from work, family, finances, and health. A certain amount of stress is normal – it motivates us. But chronic stress damages our bodies and minds. The good news is that we can manage it with simple techniques. Let’s start with the biology.

When you perceive a threat, your brain triggers the ‘fight or flight’ response. Your heart rate increases, muscles tense, and cortisol  rises. This response evolved for physical dangers – like a predator. But today, the threats are psychological – a deadline, a difficult email, a traffic jam. Your body still reacts as if you’re being chased by a lion. Over time, high cortisol leads to high blood pressure, poor sleep, weight gain, anxiety, and depression.

So what can you do? The first and most effective is physical activity. Exercise releases endorphins – natural mood elevators. Even a 10‑minute brisk walk reduces cortisol for up to 2 hours. Ideally, aim for 30 minutes of moderate activity  five times a week. If you can’t, break it into 10‑minute chunks. Exercise also improves sleep, which in turn reduces stress.

Second, breathing. When stressed, you tend to breathe shallowly and rapidly. That signals your brain that something is wrong, perpetuating the cycle. Try ‘box breathing’: inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. Repeat for 2 minutes. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system – the ‘rest and digest’ mode. Do this whenever you feel overwhelmed – before a meeting, after a difficult call, or in bed before sleep.

Third, mindfulness. This doesn’t mean emptying your mind. It means paying attention to the present moment without judgement. For example, while drinking tea, focus on the warmth of the cup, the aroma, the taste. When your mind wanders , gently bring it back. There are free apps like Smiling Mind or Insight Timer with 5‑minute guided exercises. Research shows that 10 minutes of mindfulness a day for 8 weeks changes brain structure – reducing the size of the amygdala  and increasing the prefrontal cortex .

Fourth, social connection. Isolating makes stress worse. Even a 5‑minute chat with a friend – in person or by phone – reduces cortisol. But avoid ‘co‑rumination’ – repeatedly complaining without problem‑solving. That actually increases stress. Instead, talk about solutions or just share a laugh. Laughter triggers endorphins and reduces stress hormones. Watch a funny video or call a friend who makes you laugh.

Fifth, sleep hygiene. Most adults need 7‑9 hours. Stress makes it hard to sleep, and poor sleep increases stress – a vicious cycle. Set a consistent bedtime and wake time, even on weekends. Avoid screens  for an hour before bed – blue light suppresses melatonin. Instead, read a paper book, listen to calm music, or take a warm bath. Keep your bedroom cool , dark, and quiet. If you can’t sleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something boring  until you feel tired. Don’t just lie there worrying.

Sixth, time management. Many stressors come from feeling overwhelmed. Use the ‘Eisenhower Matrix’: sort tasks into four boxes – urgent and important , important but not urgent , urgent but not important , and neither . Most people spend too much time on urgent but not important tasks – like answering every email immediately. Learn to say no. Also, break large tasks into small steps. ‘Write report’ is daunting; ‘open document and write heading’ is easy.

Seventh, challenge unhelpful thoughts. Stress often comes from irrational beliefs. For example, ‘I must be perfect’ or ‘everything is going wrong’. Ask yourself: ‘Is that really true? What’s the evidence? What would I tell a friend in this situation?’ This is cognitive behavioural therapy . You can learn basic CBT from free online resources or books like ‘Feeling Good’ by David Burns.

Eighth, diet. Caffeine and sugar can mimic stress – they increase heart rate and cause energy crashes. Reduce coffee to one cup in the morning. Avoid energy drinks and sugary snacks. Instead, eat regular meals with protein and complex carbohydrates – like oatmeal, eggs, or nuts. Stay hydrated – dehydration causes fatigue and irritability.

Ninth, nature. Spending time in green space reduces cortisol. Even a view of trees from a window helps. If you can, walk in a park on your lunch break. If not, bring a plant into your office. In one study, hospital patients with a view of trees recovered faster than those with a view of a brick wall.

Tenth, professional help. If stress is interfering with your work, relationships, or sleep for more than a few weeks, see your GP. They can refer you for counselling – often free on the NHS . In some cases, medication like SSRIs can help, especially if stress has become depression or anxiety disorder. There’s no shame – it’s a medical condition.

To summarise: move your body, breathe deeply, practice mindfulness, connect with others, sleep well, manage time, challenge thoughts, eat healthily, spend time in nature, and seek help if needed. Start with one technique – just five minutes of breathing today. Small changes compound.

Welcome back to ‘Pet Talk’. I’m Rachel. Last week we covered rabbits; today it’s cats. Cats are the most popular pet in the UK – over 10 million pet cats. But they can be mysterious and sometimes frustrating. Let’s solve common behaviour problems.

First, scratching furniture. Cats scratch to mark territory , to stretch muscles, and to remove old claw sheaths. You cannot stop scratching entirely – it’s natural. But you can redirect it. Provide a scratching post – tall enough  and stable . Sisal rope or corrugated cardboard are best – carpet is less attractive. Place the post near the furniture they scratch. Use positive reinforcement – when they use the post, give a treat. You can also use double‑sided sticky tape on furniture – cats hate sticky paws. Never declaw – it’s amputation of the last bone, causes pain and behavioural issues, and is illegal in the UK.

Second, inappropriate urination . This is the #1 reason cats are surrendered to shelters. First, rule out medical issues – urinary tract infections, bladder stones, kidney disease. Take the cat to the vet. If medical causes are ruled out, it’s behavioural.

transcript.speaker: causes
transcript.text:
dirty litter box , wrong type of litter , location , number of boxes . Also, stress – new baby, new pet, moving house. Use a synthetic pheromone diffuser  to reduce anxiety. Clean soiled areas with enzymatic cleaner – not bleach or ammonia .

Third, aggression towards other cats. Cats are territorial. Introduce new cats slowly – keep them in separate rooms for a week, swap bedding to exchange scents, then allow supervised visual contact, then short interactions. Never force them together. Provide multiple resources – food bowls, water bowls, litter boxes, high perches – so they don’t compete. Use a ‘catification’ – shelves and tunnels to increase vertical space. If fighting occurs, do not intervene with hands – use a loud noise or a pillow to separate. Consider consulting a behaviourist.

Fourth, night waking. Cats are crepuscular – most active at dawn and dusk. If your cat wakes you at 3 AM, do not give attention or food – that rewards the behaviour. Instead, have a predictable play session before bed  followed by a meal – this mimics the ‘hunt, catch, kill, eat’ cycle. Provide automatic feeders for early morning. Also, ignore the cat – get earplugs. It may take weeks, but they will learn that you don’t respond.

Fifth, counter surfing – jumping on kitchen counters. Cats love high places. Make counters unrewarding: remove food, cover with sticky tape or aluminium foil . Provide an acceptable high place nearby – a cat tree or shelf. When the cat uses that, reward. Never punish  – that damages trust. Instead, use ‘remote correction’ – a motion‑activated air puff  that startles but doesn’t harm.

Sixth, excessive meowing. Some breeds are vocal . But increased vocalisation can signal pain, hunger, or cognitive decline in older cats. Check with vet. If medical causes ruled out, ignore attention‑seeking meows – do not speak, look, or feed. Only give attention when quiet. Also, increase environmental enrichment – puzzle feeders, window perches, rotation of toys. A bored cat meows.

Seventh, biting during petting. Many cats have ‘petting‑induced aggression’ – they bite after a few strokes because they become overstimulated. Learn your cat’s tolerance – watch for tail twitching, ears flattening, or skin rippling. Stop before the bite. Pet only on head and chin – avoid belly and back. If your cat bites, freeze – don’t pull away . Slowly remove your hand. Then ignore for a few minutes.

Now, prevent problems with proper environment. Cats need: litter box , scratching post, high perches, hiding places , interactive toys, and daily play. Indoor cats also need window access – a catio  is ideal but even a window hammock helps. Provide two water bowls – one away from food – cats prefer running water, so a cat fountain encourages drinking.

Finally, remember that cats are not small dogs. They don’t respond to punishment or dominance. Positive reinforcement  works best. If you have persistent problems, consult a vet or a certified cat behaviourist – many offer online consultations.

Next week: we’ll talk about fish keeping. Until then, happy cat parenting.

Good evening. I’m Mark, and I work in cybersecurity. Tonight I want to talk about online scams – how to recognise them and how to protect yourself. Scammers are getting more sophisticated, but the same basic tricks have been used for decades – just delivered digitally. Let’s start with the most common: phishing emails.

Phishing emails pretend to be from a legitimate company – your bank, PayPal, Amazon, or even HMRC. They often say there’s a problem with your account, a package delivery failed, or you’ve won a prize. They include a link that takes you to a fake website that looks real. You enter your login details, and the scammer steals them. How to spot phishing: check the sender’s email address – not just the name. Amazon emails come from @amazon.co.uk, not @amaz0n‑support.ru. Hover over links – the real web address appears. Don’t click – type the company’s address yourself. Also, legitimate companies never ask for passwords or PINs by email.

Second, phone scams. ‘Vishing’  – you get a call from ‘your bank’ saying there’s fraud on your account. They ask you to move money to a ‘safe account’. That’s always a scam – no bank ever asks you to move money. Hang up. Call your bank back on a number from your bank card – not the number the caller gave you. Also, ‘tech support’ scams – a pop‑up on your computer says ‘Microsoft warning – virus detected. Call this number.’ It’s a scam. Microsoft does not call you. Never give remote access to your computer to an unsolicited caller.

Third, text message scams . Texts claiming to be from your delivery company – ‘Your parcel could not be delivered. Click to reschedule.’ The link steals your details. Or ‘Your bank account has been locked. Click to verify.’ Again, don’t click. Forward suspicious texts to 7726 . Your mobile provider will investigate.

Fourth, romance scams. You meet someone online – dating app or social media. They build a relationship over weeks or months, then need money urgently – for a plane ticket, medical emergency, or business problem. They always have a reason they can’t meet in person. Never send money to someone you haven’t met face‑to‑face. The average victim loses £10,000. Report to Action Fraud.

Fifth, investment scams. You see an ad for ‘get rich quick’ – cryptocurrency, forex trading, or binary options. They promise high returns with no risk. The ‘investment platform’ looks professional, but when you try to withdraw, you can’t – your money is gone. Always check the Financial Conduct Authority register – legitimate firms are listed. If they’re not, it’s a scam. Be especially wary of ‘pump and dump’ groups on Telegram or WhatsApp – they promote a worthless stock, you buy, they sell, you lose.

Sixth, ‘Hi Mum’ scams. You get a message from a number you don’t recognise: ‘Mum, I broke my phone. This is my new number. Can you send £500 for a new phone?’ The scammer pretends to be your child. Always call your child on their real number to verify. If you can’t reach them, ask a question only they would know – ‘What’s the name of our dog?’ Scammers can’t answer.

Seventh, fake shopping websites. You find a bargain – a new iPhone for £300, designer shoes for £50. The site looks real but has spelling errors, no contact address, and payment only by bank transfer . You pay, and nothing arrives. Always use credit cards for online shopping – you have Section 75 protection for purchases over £100. Check reviews of the site – search ‘site name + scam’. Use a site like Trustpilot.

Eighth, invoice and mandate fraud. You get an email that looks like from a supplier – ‘Our bank details have changed. Please pay future invoices to this new account.’ The email is fake. Always verify by calling the supplier on a known number – not the number in the email. This scam has cost businesses millions.

Ninth, data breaches. Scammers use stolen passwords from one site to try on others. So if you use the same password for Amazon and your bank, a leak at Amazon gives them access to your bank. Use unique passwords for every site – use a password manager like Bitwarden or LastPass . Also, enable two‑factor authentication  wherever possible – a code from an app or text message in addition to your password.

Tenth, what to do if you’re scammed. First, don’t be ashamed – anyone can be fooled. Report to Action Fraud  or Police Scotland . Contact your bank immediately – they may be able to reverse the transaction under the Contingent Reimbursement Model . Change all compromised passwords. Monitor your credit report – you can get free reports from Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion.

Finally, prevention. Be sceptical – if it seems too good to be true, it is. Never click links in unsolicited messages. Never give personal information over the phone. Use a spam filter. Keep your computer and phone updated. And talk to older relatives – they are often targeted. Share this information.

Remember, scammers rely on urgency and fear. Slow down. Verify. Don’t be rushed. Thank you.
